title: Convergence-Weighted Aggregation of Cross-Exchange Prediction Markets: A Dependency-Aware Index for Combining Prices Across Kalshi, Polymarket, Manifold, Metaculus, and Long-Tail Venues
items.abstract: <jats:p>Modern prediction-market venues — Kalshi, Polymarket, Manifold, Metaculus, and a long tail of newer exchanges — increasingly host overlapping markets on identical world events. Naive aggregation methods (simple or volume-weighted means, Hanson-style market-scoring averages, information-diversity weighted aggregators) treat each venue as a conditionally independent source given the resolution outcome. This assumption is violated in practice by three documented mechanisms: cross-exchange copy-trading bots, shared news flow that drives all venues simultaneously after material announcements, and arbitrageurs whose activity compresses cross-exchange variance below the level that would reflect genuine informational dispersion. Under this dependence, weighted-mean aggregators are biased and overconfident in the contamination regimes a deployer cares about most. We adapt the Index of Convergence Multi-epistemic (ICM) framework, originally developed for cross-disciplinary scientific aggregation (Stanisljevic, 2026), to the prediction-market setting. ICM augments naive aggregation with five components — agreement (A), direction (D), uncertainty overlap (U), perturbation invariance (C), and a dependency penalty (Pi) — yielding a convergence-weighted estimator that decouples genuine cross-source agreement from cross-source contagion. Within Pi, the lead-lag primitive Pi_L is the load-bearing component for the empirical bias-reduction result. We evaluate ICM-weighted aggregation against three baselines (naive mean, volume-weighted mean, Satopaa-Pemantle-Ungar logit-pool) on (i) synthetic experiments under each contamination mechanism in isolation, (ii) hybrid backtests with real Polymarket trajectories, and (iii) a strict cross-exchange backtest on binary markets where Polymarket and Manifold both have hourly history. Synthetic experiments confirm bias-reduction under copy-trading contamination (Mechanism I); the result is regime-targeted rather than uniformly dominant. The strict cross-exchange backtest is reported with the explicit caveat that ICM degenerates to the equal-weighted naive mean at V = 2 listing venues, so the reported Polymarket+Manifold result tests the surrounding pipeline but not the pair-discriminating ICM machinery. Forward-looking evaluation across additional exchanges (Kalshi via authenticated API, plus Metaculus and the long-tail venues) is planned with rolling collection commencing May 2026. Conjecture 1 (asymptotic bias reduction under contamination) is supported by a mechanism-by-mechanism heuristic argument; the formalization of the asymptotic-rate proof is left to follow-up.</jats:p>

title: Cryptocurrency Prediction Markets through the Derivatives Lens: Evidence from Kalshi and Polymarket
items.abstract: <jats:p>Cryptocurrency prediction markets have grown rapidly, yet their prices have been studied almost exclusively as probability forecasts. Because the binary contracts traded on these platforms are structurally identical to cash-or-nothing digital options, the standard derivatives pricing toolkit applies directly. We exploit this equivalence on 113,338 Bitcoin and Ethereum contracts traded on Kalshi and Polymarket between September 2025 and February 2026, extracting implied volatility surfaces, risk-neutral densities, and variance risk premia from prediction market prices for the first time. Risk-neutral skewness recovered from multi-strike Kalshi events is near zero, and the implied volatility smile is pronounced and roughly symmetric, contrasting with the persistent left-skewed smirk that crash-protection demand produces in equity index options. Implied variance exceeds realized variance across all contract series, documenting a positive variance risk premium in prediction markets. The VRP differs markedly across platforms, with Polymarket&apos;s roughly 16 times larger than Kalshi&apos;s, a pattern consistent with Polymarket&apos;s forward-start contract design, which anchors pre-window prices near 0.50 and inflates implied variance. Calibration analysis shows that both venues are systematically underconfident, with Polymarket exhibiting more severe probability distortion. A cross-platform comparison of matched contracts is consistent with much of this divergence reflecting the structural distinction between fixed-strike and forward-start contracts. The derivatives framework reveals risk pricing information in prediction markets that probability-based analysis alone cannot detect.</jats:p>

title: Arbitrage Analysis in Polymarket NBA Markets
items.abstract: <jats:p>While decentralized prediction markets like Polymarket have gained significant traction, their market microstructure and high-frequency pricing efficiency remain underexplored. This paper conducts a systematic empirical analysis of algorithmic arbitrage within Polymarket's NBA game markets. By reconstructing continuous market states from over 75 million limit order book snapshots across 173 games, we evaluate the frequency, duration, and profitability of both single-market and combinatorial arbitrage opportunities. Our findings demonstrate profound microstructural efficiency. Single-market anomalies are exceedingly rare, yielding only 7 executable in-game episodes that persist for a median duration of just 3.6 seconds. Combinatorial inefficiencies are more frequent, producing 290 active episodes overwhelmingly concentrated in the final minutes of live play. While combinatorial execution yields a statistically meaningful median return of 101 basis points, we find that the theoretical "Middle" jackpot is never empirically realized. Furthermore, execution is severely bottlenecked by shallow order book depth, with 76.9% of combinatorial opportunities constrained to an average executable size of just 14.8 shares. Ultimately, while executable mispricings exist, they are structurally bounded by liquidity, confining risk-free extraction strictly to the retail scale.</jats:p>

title: Priority Fees and Hedge Design in Cross-Venue Arbitrage between Centralized and Decentralized Exchanges
items.abstract: <jats:p>Arbitrage between centralized (CEX) and decentralized (DEX) exchanges is often modelled as if both legs were executed simultaneously at quoted prices. In practice, the CEX leg can be filled immediately, while the DEX leg waits for block inclusion. We study this mismatch in a model where the trader chooses a priority fee and a linear CEX hedge after observing an arbitrage signal. The priority fee changes the confirmation-time distribution; the hedge changes the exposure during the wait. A mean--variance benchmark gives closed-form rules for both controls: the hedge is a projection on the CEX instrument, while the fee equates marginal gas cost with the value of shorter exposure. A stochastic-control version with execution intensity leads, after a CRRA reduction, to a one-dimensional Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation in the CEX--DEX log spread. Empirical analysis is used strictly to calibrate magnitudes. In low-gas 2026 data, the optimal fee is usually the lower admissible bid. In congested gas regimes, the formula raises the fee because waiting risk and gas costs both enter the same first-order condition.</jats:p>

title: Liquidity Fragmentation and the Price Impact of ETF Flows: A Model of Cross-Venue Arbitrage in Cryptocurrency Markets
items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper develops a theoretical model of price impact in fragmented cryptocurrency markets, where ETF-driven order flow must be routed across heterogeneous exchanges with varying liquidity depth. Extending Kyle (1985) to a multi-venue setting, I derive an aggregate price impact function that is linear for moderate flows but becomes convex when flows exceed any single venue's capacity. The model generates four testable predictions: (1) linear price impact for moderate flows, (2) volatility amplification, (3) permanent price impact with no reversal, and (4) flow-driven return momentum. Using 563 trading days of net flow data from all U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs (January 2024-April 2026), sourced from Farside Investors, I confirm all four predictions. An instrumental variables approach using lagged flows (first-stage F = 89.5) yields a causal price impact of 0.20% per $100 million net inflow (t = 2.65), roughly half the OLS estimate (0.41%, t = 10.38), indicating substantial same-day simultaneity between flows and returns. Volatility amplifies the price impact (t = 2.51), current flows predict next-day returns (t = 2.26), and there is no evidence of price reversal at any horizon up to 12 months (250 trading days)-in stark contrast to the quarterly reversal documented in equity markets by Lou (2012). The flow-return relationship is stable across subperiods and robust to the exclusion of extreme flows. These findings have implications for the design of ETF products linked to fragmented underlying assets.</jats:p>

title: Who Profits in Binary Prediction Markets? Maker-Taker Dynamics, Behavioral Bias, and Sentiment Arbitrage on Kalshi
items.abstract: <jats:p>Whether liquidity providers in binary prediction markets systematically profit from uninformed order flow, and whether behavioral biases sustain that profit, remain open empirical questions. We address them using 72.1 million executed trades ($18.3B notional) on Kalshi from July 2021 through November 2025, supplemented by 404.5 million on-chain trades from Polymarket, applying volume-weighted return decomposition, calibration analysis, OLS regression, and paired t-tests. A statistically significant Favorite-Longshot Bias (FLSB) emerges on both platforms, but with a cross-platform contrast: Kalshi longshots are overpriced (δ b &lt; 0, p &lt; 0.001 for all sub-25% buckets) while Polymarket favorites above 55% implied probability are systematically underpriced (δ b &gt; 0, t up to 361), implicating market design as the key moderating factor. On the supply side, makers earn +0.83 percentage points (pp) in volumeweighted returns (p = 0.0055), constituting a $142.5M wealth transfer that exceeds estimated bid-ask spread compensation by 0.13 pp. This alpha is not uniform: it ranges from +0.29 pp in Finance to +3.01 pp in World Events, with high-volume categories spanning +0.82 pp (Sports) to +1.78 pp (Media), consistent with adverse selection varying by information environment. On the demand side, takers allocate 63.8% of capital to YES contracts despite earning 0.32 pp less than NO-side takers, an affirmative framing bias unexplained by differential risk. Contrary to efficiency-convergence predictions, maker alpha trends upward at +8.21 bp/month (R 2 = 0.70) as retail participation grows. A sport-level decomposition of the dominant sports category (74% of volume) reveals maker alpha ranging from +0.18 pp in MLB to +3.43 pp in UFC/Boxing, with no significant time-to-resolution decay (p = 0.88), providing direct evidence of persistent fandriven sentiment arbitrage. Taken together, these findings indicate that binary prediction markets structurally disadvantage uninformed retail participants and call for targeted disclosure requirements and calibration-oriented regulatory oversight.</jats:p>

title: Choose Your Corporate Law: Domicile, Listing Venue and Governance Arbitrage in the Australian Public Market Should founders incorporate in Australia before an ASX IPO?
items.abstract: <jats:p>Access to the Australian public capital market and subjection to Australian corporate law are commonly assumed to travel together. They do not. A company can obtain the principal benefits of an ASX quotation-Australian institutional and superannuation capital, liquidity, analyst coverage, index eligibility and an Australian shareholder base-while its directors and remuneration arrangements remain governed by the corporate law of New Zealand, Delaware, Nevada or Ireland. This paper reframes that possibility as a corporate design choice, asking the question as a founder, board or adviser would: for a company seeking Australian public capital, what is the optimal combination of place of incorporation, primary listing venue and ASX admission category? Drawing on ASX's July 2026 Foreign Entity Report, the paper maps the architecture of that choice and develops six migration case studies-Xero, Life360, Anteris Technologies, Incannex Healthcare, Nova Minerals and James Hardie, with Light &amp; Wonder as the inbound counter-case-using Australia's two-strikes remuneration regime as the cleanest demonstration that economically similar ASX-listed companies face materially different governance constraints by domicile alone. Twelve testable hypotheses, a practitioner decision matrix and policy implications for a market in which corporate law has become elective complete the analysis.</jats:p>

title: Regulatory Arbitrage in Cross-Border Crowdfunding
items.abstract: In the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis, small businesses found it increasingly difficult to raise funds. As a response, equity crowdfunding has emerged as a viable alternative for sourcing capital to support innovative, entrepreneurial ideas and ventures. A number of securities regulators across the world have dealt with, or are in the process of dealing with, equity crowdfunding as a disruptive innovation to established processes of corporate fundraising. However, most equity crowdfunding regulations do not take into account one critical aspect of crowdfunding—that of cross-border crowdfunding. Using a comparative analysis of a number of jurisdictions around the world in their treatment of equity crowdfunding, this chapter argues that in jurisdictions where crowdfunding activities are unregulated or have a low threshold of regulations, the opportunities arising from the resultant regulatory arbitrage could then be used by fund-seeking companies based in jurisdictions where crowdfunding is prohibited or highly regulated.

title: Order-flow Provenance, Informed Entry, and Cross-venue Spreads
items.abstract: <jats:p>Brokers route retail-labeled order flow to wholesalers, while exchanges receive the residue. We model provenance as a noisy binary classifier in a one-round, symmetric two-state Glosten-Milgrom market with endogenous informed entry. At fixed participation, the classifier lowers aggregate uninformed trading cost relative to pooling by half the value gap times the variance of the label posterior; hence Blackwell sharpening weakly raises this fixed-participation saving. With free entry, Blackwell sharpening weakly reduces informed entry and average uninformed execution costs. Its venue-level incidence is asymmetric. Every orientation-preserving sharpening lowers the retail break-even spread, whereas its effect on the exchange spread decomposes into retail- and exchange-purification margins with a closed-form threshold. Routing more uninformed flow to the retail label widens the exchange spread at every retention level below quote matching and leaves it unchanged under quote matching. Better detection of informed traders behind that label can narrow or widen it depending on the arrival-based venue mass. Greater retention reduces informed entry but raises the average uninformed-trader execution cost toward the pooled-market level. Historical and pre-amendment Rule 605 moments illustrate the model-to-data mapping and show which incidence comparisons require an external normalization or an arrival-based mass not identified by covered-volume shares.</jats:p>

title: Regulatory Arbitrage in Cross Border Crowdfunding
items.abstract: <jats:p>In the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis, small businesses found it increasingly difficult to raise funds. Equity crowdfunding has emerged as a viable alternative for sourcing capital to support innovative, entrepreneurial ventures. Equity crowdfunding merges the complexity of public funding, with the systemic risks of venture capital funding.<br><br>A key responsibility of any securities regulator is that of investor protection. Securities laws, involving stringent eligibility criteria for fundraising companies and detailed disclosure requirements have been instrumental in mitigating risks for public retail investors to some extent. A number of securities regulators across the world have dealt with, or are in the process of dealing with equity crowdfunding as a disruptive innovation to established processes of corporate fundraising. However, most equity crowdfunding regulations do not take into account one critical aspect of crowdfunding - that of cross-border crowdfunding.<br><br>I argue that in jurisdictions where crowdfunding activities are unregulated or have a low threshold of regulations, the opportunities arising from the resultant regulatory arbitrage could then be used by fund-seeking companies based in jurisdictions where crowdfunding is prohibited or highly regulated. As a result, securities regulators must work together to derive minimum standards of acceptable behavior in cross-border crowdfunding markets.<br><br>This is a draft of a chapter that has been accepted for publication by Oxford University Press in the  Oxford Handbook of IPOs edited by Douglas Cummings and Sofia Johan published in 2018. An earlier version of this paper was drafted as part of a visiting research fellowship at the Melbourne Law School. The author is grateful to Mr Lakshay Garg, BBALLB Class of 2013, Jindal Global Law School for his research assistance.</jats:p>

title: Polymarket-v1 Database
items.abstract: <jats:p>We introduce the Polymarket-v1 Database: the complete on-chain trade archive of Polymarket's first-generation CTF Exchange on Polygon, spanning 2022-11-21 to 2026-04-28 and covering the full contract lifecycle from first settlement to natural termination. The dataset comprises 1.20 billion trade records across 1.30 million markets with $61 billion in nominal volume. Its defining feature is all ground-truth aggressor direction derived from the blockchain settlement layer, a property unavailable in existing prediction market archives, which rely on heuristic inference. We use this truth-aligned archive to benchmark standard microstructure tools and document three findings. First, the tick rule and bulk volume classification achieve nearrandom aggregate accuracy (49.83% and 50.51%), but this masks a systematic, correctable price-level gradient driven by positive trade direction autocorrelation and concentrated market-making-two structural features of prediction markets that violate the mean-reversion assumption embedded in classical classifiers. Second, these classification errors propagate into downstream metrics: inferred VPIN diverges substantially from ground-truth VPIN, and OFI estimates are directionally biased, with material consequences for Transaction Cost Analysis. Third, ground-truth microstructure quality predicts forecasting performance in ways that classification-based proxies cannot recover: True VPIN positively predicts Brier scores, while Gibbs spread negatively predicts them-a selection effect reflecting that high-spread niche markets attract informed specialists rather than noise traders. Replacing ground-truth metrics with classified proxies attenuates both relationships, illustrating that measurement accuracy at the transaction level is a prerequisite for reliable inference about prediction market design and probability calibration. The dataset is publicly available.</jats:p>

title: Cross-Listed Shares Arbitrage and Price Formation
items.abstract: <jats:p>We investigate the behavior of prices of shares of the same company listed on the home and ADR markets. Our study brings together insights from two separate fields of research: the pricing of dual listed shares and the price formation for cointegrated series. Both arbitrage and rational expectations arguments may be used to argue the exchange rate adjusted prices of the securities should be the same or at least move in sync to the extent there are no possibilities of risk-adjusted abnormal profits. The literature presents two approaches to the problem at hand: 1) test the hypothesis using a returns regression and 2) compare prices directly. We propose cointegration as a new tool to analyze this issue. We find strong evidence that the hypothesis of Price Parity should be tested using cointegration. Our analysis leads to the conclusion that there are no profits to be made in this market and that reported anomalies are due to the erroneous interpretation of the returns regression analysis. Our analysis of the regression results show that regression coefficients are more significant in the presence of cointegration than without cointegration, which is exactly the opposite of  the original hypothesis.  Cointegration also provides additional insight about the price formation of the issue. This is the first study of price formation of cross-listed shares and we use the approach of Gonzalo and Granger (1995). The evidence from the model is anomalous in the sense that price formation for European stocks occurs on NYSE despite the relatively small volumes of trading. This is attributed to non-anticipated news releases after market close and  may have very important implications for fund managers wishing to rebalance their portfolios subsequent to a non-anticipated news release.</jats:p>

title: Cross-Listing and Arbitrage without Overlapping Time
items.abstract: <jats:p>Chinese firms tend to cross-list in different equity markets. The first wave of studies after the re-establishment of the stock market in the early 1990s indicated that cross-listing practices do not necessarily translate into arbitrage profit. This chapter examines the possibility of arbitrage profits for 14 cross-listed Chinese stocks traded on both their home exchanges (Hong Kong Main Board) and NYSE in the form of ADRs without overlapped trading hours. A simple trading strategy was developed with the consideration of four scenarios. The results indicate that a monthly return from 0.5 percent to 3.8 percent could be obtained using the simple strategy when transaction costs are considered.</jats:p>

title: Centralized–decentralized exchange funding rate arbitrage as a basis trade: risk decomposition, stress testing, and portfolio construction under venue uncertainty
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Funding rate arbitrage between centralized and decentralized cryptocurrency exchanges is often described as a low-risk carry strategy, but this description is incomplete because the trade can fail through funding-spread compression, imperfect cross-venue hedging, execution frictions, forced liquidation, and settlement or smart-contract disruption. This paper asks how CEX-DEX funding rate arbitrage should be modelled as a basis trade, which risk channels dominate its performance, and how leverage and venue choice should be controlled under stress. Using Binance Futures funding rates for BTC, ETH, and SOL from January 2021 to December 2024 and synthetic DEX funding rates designed to isolate oracle lag, structural spread, and higher DEX-rate noise, the paper develops a covariance-aware five-component risk decomposition, a Brinson-style PnL attribution, a Cox survival model for liquidation risk, historical stress tests, CVaR portfolio optimization with venue haircuts, and Monte Carlo tail-risk analysis. A protocol-data robustness exercise using observed dYdX v4 funding rates over its available overlapping window distinguishes the framework’s controlled scenario results from evidence based on an operating DEX. The results show that net annualized returns are driven mainly by funding carry, but that these returns are highly assumption-sensitive and should not be interpreted as frictionless arbitrage profits. Funding and residual market risk account for the largest variance shares, leverage and volatility regime dominate liquidation hazard, and stress tests show that counterparty-risk episodes are more damaging than purely directional price crashes. The paper contributes a transparent framework for position sizing, leverage limits, and venue allocation in cross-venue crypto basis trades.</jats:p>

title: Resiliency: Cross-Venue Dynamics with Hawkes Processes
items.abstract: <jats:p>Market fragmentation and technological advances increasing the speed of trading altered the functioning and stability of global equity limit order markets. Taking market resiliency as an indicator of market quality, we investigate how resilient are trading venues in a high-frequency environment with cross-venue fragmented order flow. Employing a Hawkes process methodology on high-frequency data for FTSE 100 stocks on LSE, a traditional exchange, and on Chi-X, an alternative venue, we find that when liquidity becomes scarce Chi-X is a less resilient venue than LSE with variations existing across stocks and time. In comparison with LSE, Chi-X has more, longer, and severer liquidity shocks. Whereas the vast majority of liquidity droughts on both venues disappear within less than one minute, the recovery is not lasting, as liquidity shocks spiral over the time dimension. Over half of the shocks on both venues are caused by spiralling. Liquidity shocks tend to spiral more on Chi-X than on LSE for large stocks suggesting that the liquidity supply on Chi-X is thinner than on LSE. Finally, a significant amount of liquidity shocks spill over cross-venue providing supporting evidence for the competition for order flow between LSE and Chi-X.</jats:p>

title: Integration Without Leadership: Cross-Venue Price Discovery in UFC Prediction Markets
items.abstract: <jats:p>Modern prediction markets are a fast-growing market structure, and sports contracts now account for around 90% of activity on Kalshi, one of the largest venues. The research attention is allocated in nearly the opposite proportion, as the previous literature concentrated on political markets, above all a single event, the 2024 United States presidential election. The sports contracts that dominate actual trading remain almost unexamined. This paper tests whether conclusions drawn from that election generalise to the markets where the volume actually is: sports contracts, trading at comparatively smaller per-market volume and liquidity. Data were collected through custom-built scrapers and a publicly distributed archive covering Kalshi and Polymarket trade histories: 281 UFC fights matched across venues over fourteen months. Contrary to the election evidence, where Polymarket led Kalshi, no venue leads price discovery in the sports setting: venue returns co-move within the same bar (+0.103 at five minutes, +0.203 at thirty minutes), while no lead-lag correlation is distinguishable from zero at any horizon. Large jumps propagate symmetrically in both directions, the single directional asymmetry fades exactly where Kalshi's one-cent grid predicts. Inter-venue gaps close within about half an hour on liquid fights, and a pre-registered test finds that aggressive order flow predicts reversal, not continuation, with a magnitude well inside fees. The findings suggest that venue leadership is not an inherent feature of fragmented prediction markets but a product of a specific configuration of salience, segmented clienteles and concentrated informed flow.</jats:p>

title: Cross-Impact and No-Dynamic-Arbitrage
items.abstract: <jats:p>We extend the “No-dynamic-arbitrage and market impact”-framework of Jim Gatheral [Quantitative Finance, 10(7): 749-759 (2010)] to the multidimensional case where trading in one asset has a cross-impact on the price of other assets. From the condition of absence of dynamical arbitrage we derive theoretical limits for the size and form of cross-impact that can be directly verified on data. For bounded decay kernels we find that cross-impact must be an odd and linear function of trading intensity and cross-impact from asset i to asset j must be equal to the one from j to i. To test these constraints we estimate cross-impact among sovereign bonds traded on the electronic platform MOT. While we find significant violations of the above symmetry condition of cross-impact, we show that these are not arbitrageable with simple strategies because of the presence of the bid-ask spread.</jats:p>

title: Stock Market Valuation, Foreign Investment, and Cross-Country Arbitrage
items.abstract: <jats:p>This study investigates the role of stock market valuation and cross-country arbitrage in shaping foreign direct and indirect investments, contingent upon a country’s stage of development.  This paper is built upon the mispricing-driven foreign investment hypotheses developed by Baker et al. (2009).  Interesting findings emerge when developed and emerging markets are considered separately.  Empirical evidence indicates that the use of relatively cheap financial capital for foreign investment is prominent among developed countries, but not so in emerging markets.  This is largely due to the extremely low level of foreign investment outflows in emerging markets and the inability of unsophisticated emerging market managers to successfully time the market.  Further investigation shows that host-country stock market valuation is an important determinant of the mode of foreign investment; investors tend to choose indirect or portfolio investment, as opposed to direct investment, when the stock market is perceived to be undervalued.  This is especially the case in emerging markets, where there is more room for misvaluation and potential arbitrage.  These findings suggest that the unique institutional features of the markets involved play an important role in shaping foreign investment and cross-country arbitrage.</jats:p>
